name: Tuna
description: While many cats love the taste of tuna, it should not be a regular part of their diet. A tiny flake of plain, cooked tuna packed in water is generally safe as a rare treat, but a diet that includes a lot of tuna can lead to serious health problems. Feeding cats raw tuna is especially risky because it contains an enzyme called thiaminase, which destroys thiamine (Vitamin B1), a nutrient essential for a healthy nervous system. A diet heavy in any kind of tuna can also lead to mercury poisoning over time, causing neurological damage. Furthermore, tuna is high in certain fats but lacks Vitamin E, an imbalance that can cause a painful inflammatory condition called steatitis, or "yellow fat disease." To be safe, never feed your cat raw tuna. Avoid tuna packed in oil or brine, as the high fat and salt content are unhealthy. Tuna should only be an occasional treat, not a meal. If your cat has been eating a tuna-heavy diet, it is best to consult with a veterinarian.
safetyNotes: Thiaminase risk: raw tuna contains thiaminase, which destroys thiamine (B1); regular raw tuna feeding causes neurological damage — weakness, head tilt, seizures
Mercury risk: tuna is high in mercury; chronic exposure causes neurological damage, kidney damage, and immune suppression
Nutritional imbalance: tuna alone lacks several essential nutrients for cats (calcium, vitamins) and is high in unsaturated fats that deplete vitamin E
Canned tuna in water (plain, no salt): safe as an occasional treat; avoid tuna in oil or with any added salt
A small piece of plain cooked tuna occasionally is fine; daily feeding is not recommended

symptoms.name: While a tiny bite of plain, cooked tuna is generally safe as a rare treat, feeding a cat a diet heavy in tuna
Steatitis (Yellow Fat Disease)
symptoms.onset: Chronic (develops over weeks to months of a diet heavy in tuna).
symptoms.notes: Tuna is extremely high in polyunsaturated fatty acids but naturally lacks adequate Vitamin E2. A heavy tuna diet depletes the cat's Vitamin E reserves, causing the fat tissue to oxidize and become painfully inflamed.

symptoms.name: Neurological Dysfunction (Methylmercury Poisoning)
symptoms.onset: Chronic (accumulates over time with regular feeding).
symptoms.notes: Because tuna is a large apex predator, it bioaccumulates high levels of methylmercury2. Cats are particularly sensitive to low doses of organic mercury, which easily crosses the blood-brain barrier and interferes with neuronal protein synthesis.

symptoms.name: Neurological Dysfunction (Thiamine Deficiency) (Note
symptoms.onset: Chronic / Delayed (typically develops within 2 to 4 weeks of a raw fish-heavy diet).
symptoms.notes: Raw tuna (such as Skipjack and Yellowfin) can contain thiaminase, an enzyme that destroys thiamine (Vitamin B1)6. Lack of thiamine halts cellular energy metabolism and causes a potentially fatal "Wernicke-like" encephalopathy.

symptoms.name: Gastrointestinal Upset and Salt Toxicosis (Note
symptoms.onset: Acute (within hours to a few days of ingestion).
symptoms.notes: Human-grade canned tuna is frequently packed in oil or high-sodium brine12. The high fat content in oil-packed tuna can trigger severe digestive upset or acute pancreatitis910.
